ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — Jacqueline du Pré Synthetic CCD

text.paragraph: Three weeks of numbness and clumsiness in the fingers of both hands, with Lhermitte's sign and fatigue, in a professional cellist of 28: examination, blood tests, and urgent MRI of the brain and spine. Concerns: For three weeks the fingers of both hands have been numb and tingling, worse on the left; she cannot feel the strings properly, loses her place on the fingerboard and has dropped her bow twice; an electric feeling runs down her back when she bends her head; tired by mid-afternoon for months; A similar month of tingling in her fingers 18 months ago was put down to overwork and stress, and settled; She wants to know what is wrong, and whether she will be able to play again. [S]

tr.td: Nitrofurantoin macrocrystals 100 mg oral capsule, one capsule by mouth twice daily with food for 5 days
One capsule twice daily for 5 days
Methylprednisolone 1000 mg injection, 1 g intravenously over one hour once daily for 3 days
Cholecalciferol (vitamin D3) 4000 unit (100 microgram) oral capsule, one capsule by mouth daily

Ocrelizumab 30 mg/mL injection: first dose as 300 mg intravenously on day 1 and day 15, then 600 mg intravenously every 6 months, with methylprednisolone 100 mg, an antihistamine and acetaminophen before each infusion
300 mg on days 1 and 15, then 600 mg every 6 months

MRI of the brain with and without gadolinium: 11 ovoid T2-hyperintense lesions, 3 mm to 9 mm, eight periventricular (several perpendicular to the ventricles), two juxtacortical and one in the right middle cerebellar peduncle; one periventricular lesion enhances; most lesions show a central vein; no mass, no meningeal enhancement

MRI of the cervical and thoracic spine with and without gadolinium (same session): a short dorsal lesion at C3 to C4, less than one vertebral segment long and occupying under half the cord's cross-section, with patchy enhancement; a second, non-enhancing lesion at T7; no cord swelling or compression

Lumbar puncture: clear fluid; white cells 6 per microliter (lymphocytes), protein 42 mg/dL, glucose normal; six oligoclonal bands in the cerebrospinal fluid not present in the serum; IgG index 0.86 (raised). Serum aquaporin-4 IgG by cell-based assay negative; HIV and syphilis serology negative
Advance care planning conversation, about 15 minutes

Occupational therapy assessment and program for hand function and fatigue: fine-motor and sensory re-education exercises for the fingers, graded return to practice in short blocks with rests, posture at the instrument, and energy management

Re-baseline MRI of the brain with and without gadolinium three months after starting ocrelizumab: no new or enlarging T2 lesions and no enhancing lesions; the previously enhancing periventricular lesion is smaller

list.item: Numbness, tingling and loss of position sense in the fingers of both hands for three weeks, worse on the left, with clumsiness that makes her lose her place on the fingerboard, an electric feeling down the spine on bending the neck (Lhermitte's sign), and fatigue; a similar month of tingling in the fingers 18 months ago settled on its own. A lesion of the cervical spinal cord must be found: MRI of the brain and spine with contrast booked this week: resolved, confirmed [S]

Relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis, active: a current relapse (partial cervical myelitis at C3 to C4 with sensory loss and clumsiness of the hands) after an earlier sensory episode; dissemination in space and time on MRI, with an enhancing cord lesion and an enhancing brain lesion; CSF-specific oligoclonal bands; aquaporin-4 antibody negative; meets the 2017 McDonald criteria and the 2024 revision; synthetic modern detail linked to her documented diagnosis: active, confirmed [S]
Vitamin D deficiency: 25-hydroxyvitamin D 16 ng/mL; replacement to correct the deficiency, not as a treatment for multiple sclerosis: active, confirmed [S]

Acute uncomplicated cystitis (Escherichia coli) seven weeks after the first ocrelizumab course, with a pseudo-relapse: two days of returning tingling in the fingers with a low fever and no new neurological deficit; resolved: resolved, confirmed [S]

tr.td: Three weeks of numbness and clumsiness in the fingers of both hands, with Lhermitte's sign and fatigue, in a professional cellist of 28: examination, blood tests, and urgent MRI of the brain and spine
Diagnosis of relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis: neurology consultation, treatment of the relapse, choice of high-efficacy disease-modifying therapy, and vaccinations before B-cell therapy
Second half-dose of the first ocrelizumab course: recovery of hand function, infusion reactions, vaccination, practice and work
Three months on ocrelizumab: re-baseline MRI, B-cell depletion, fatigue, vitamin D and hand function
Six months: first 600 mg dose of ocrelizumab, no evidence of disease activity, immunoglobulins, vaccination response, pregnancy planning and her return to performing
Same-day sick visit for cystitis with a pseudo-relapse
Periodic adult preventive visit on B-cell therapy

code.displayName: Periodic reevaluation and management of healthy individual

tr.td: Neurology (multiple sclerosis) consultation within two weeks to review the MRI with her and make a diagnosis and plan

Urgent work-up of a sensory syndrome of both hands with Lhermitte's sign: MRI of the brain and cervical and thoracic spine with gadolinium within a week; blood count, chemistry, vitamin B12 and TSH; lumbar puncture for oligoclonal bands if the MRI is suggestive; return at once for weakness, unsteadiness, loss of bladder control or loss of vision

Relapse treatment: methylprednisolone 1 g intravenously daily for three days for a relapse that limits her hand function, after excluding infection; occupational therapy for hand function and energy management

Early high-efficacy disease-modifying therapy with ocrelizumab: 300 mg intravenously on days 1 and 15, then 600 mg every six months, with premedication; chosen over natalizumab because the JCV antibody is positive and over ofatumumab at her preference for twice-yearly infusions; before the first dose, hepatitis B screening, varicella and measles immunity, immunoglobulins, a pregnancy test, and inactivated vaccines at least two weeks ahead; contraception during treatment
Vitamin D: cholecalciferol 4000 units daily to correct deficiency, with a level after three months; not as a treatment for multiple sclerosis

Monitoring on ocrelizumab: re-baseline MRI of the brain three to six months after starting, then yearly; blood count and immunoglobulins before each dose; infection and pseudo-relapse teaching; pregnancy planning, with conception timed after a dose

Fatigue, mood and work: screening for depression and sleep problems at each visit, plain explanations with written information, and a plan built around her practice, performing and teaching; she decides who is told and who receives each note
MRI of the brain and spine within one week and a neurology diagnosis within three weeks
MRI in three days, lumbar puncture in a week, diagnosis and consultation at two weeks
High-efficacy disease-modifying therapy started within six weeks of diagnosis, after screening and vaccinations
Ocrelizumab started three weeks after the diagnosis; PCV20, recombinant zoster and hepatitis B vaccines given first
Nine-hole peg times back to within 10 percent of normal in both hands, and full practice resumed
19.0 seconds right and 20.5 seconds left at three months; practicing three hours a day
No evidence of disease activity at six months (no relapse, no new or enhancing MRI lesion, no disability progression)
No relapse; re-baseline MRI with no new or enhancing lesions; examination stable
